rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmala in 27:30 is plainly part of that verse and certainly Qurʾān by explicit, unanimously established transmission; surah-opening basmalas raise a separate question.
rows.anchor: Sûre-i Neml’in bu âyetinin bir cüz’ü olduğu kemâl-i sarâhatle mâlumdur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether the basmala written before surahs is a verse within them, a verse-part, or an independent Qurʾānic unit is a scholarly issue tied to faith, prayer, and recitation.
rows.anchor: bu besmelenin ta‘yîn-i Kur’ânîsi tefsirde ve ilm-i usûlde bir mes’ele-i ilmiye teşkil etmiştir

rows.speaker: Saîd b. Cübeyr, Zührî, Atâ, İbn Mübârek
rows.claim: These early authorities hold that every surah-opening basmala is one verse of that surah, yielding 113 such verses in the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: Saîd b. Cübeyr, Zührî, Atâ, İbn Mübârek hazerâtı besmelenin başında bulunduğu her sûreden birer âyet

rows.speaker: İmam Şâfiî ve ashâbı
rows.claim: In his later position al-Shāfiʿī and his followers adopt the view that each surah-opening basmala is a verse.
rows.anchor: Kavl-i cedîdinde İmam Şâfiî hazretleri ve ashâbı bu mezheb üzerindedirler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this view the basmala is al-Fātiḥa’s first verse, while anʿamta ʿalayhim is not a verse ending, so they recite the basmala aloud in prayer.
rows.anchor: O hâlde Fâtiha’nın yedi âyetinden birincisi besmeledir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their argument is that the early community wrote the basmalas in the muṣḥafs while preserving the Qurʾān’s purity and excluding even Āmīn.
rows.anchor: selef bu besmeleleri mushaflarda tesbit etmişler, bununla beraber Kur’ân’ın tecrîdini tavsiye eylemişler

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that omitting the basmala omits 114 verses from God’s Book.
rows.anchor: Besmele’yi terk eden Kitâbullah’dan yüz on dört âyet terk etmiş olur

rows.speaker: Ebû Hüreyre
rows.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet counted al-Fātiḥa as seven verses and named the basmala as its first.
rows.anchor: Fâtihatü’l-Kitâb yedi âyettir, bunların evveli بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ

rows.speaker: Ümmü Seleme
rows.claim: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet counted the basmala together with al-ḥamdu lillāh as one verse.
rows.anchor: Resûlullah Fâtiha’yı okudu ve بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ’i bir âyet saydı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shāfiʿī argument concludes that even if the basmala is not a whole verse of al-Fātiḥa, it is part of a verse, making its recitation obligatory and audible in prayer.
rows.anchor: Fâtiha’dan bir âyet değilse cüz’-i âyettir. Ve binâen‘aleyh namazda kıraati farzdır ve cehr olunur

rows.speaker: Ahmed b. Hanbel
rows.claim: Like al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal has two transmitted positions, reflecting uncertainty between the two hadith reports.
rows.anchor: Ahmed b. Hanbel hazretlerinden de bu iki hadis beyninde tereddüdle iki rivayet mevcuddur

rows.speaker: İmam Mâlik
rows.claim: Mālik holds that opening basmalas are neither part of al-Fātiḥa or other surahs nor a separate Qurʾānic portion; they are written for separation and blessing and are not recited in prayer.
rows.anchor: besmelelerin ne Fâtiha ve ne sâir sûrelerden, ne de bütün Kur’an’dan bir cüz’-i mahsus olmadığına

rows.speaker: İmam Mâlik
rows.claim: Mālik bases his view on the need for Qurʾānic status to be explicit and mutawātir at every locus and on the practice of Medina’s people.
rows.anchor: ehl-i Medine’nin teâmülüne istinad ederek sûre evvellerindeki besmelelerin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound Ḥanafī position reconciles the other arguments: each opening basmala is an independent Qurʾānic verse, revealed to separate surahs and for blessing, and belongs to none of them.
rows.anchor: Evâil-i süverdeki besmele başlı başına bir âyet-i münferide olarak Kur’an’dandır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the basmala is independent rather than part of al-Fātiḥa, reciting it in every prayer is not obligatory like al-Fātiḥa, though beginning each recitation and important undertaking with it is sunnah.
rows.anchor: her kıraatin ve her emr-i mühimmin bidâyetinde okunması sünnettir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanafīs say it at the start of each prayer unit’s recitation, not in the middle, and recite it silently even in audible prayers so it will not appear part of the surah.
rows.anchor: namazın her rekatında, kıraatin evvelinde okuruz, ortasında okumayız

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outwardly the basmala has four words, but in reality and legal reckoning it has seven because bāʾ and the two definite articles count as words, while bāʾ also implies a verb and its agent.
rows.anchor: Besmele zâhirde بِسْمِ، اللّٰهِّٰ، الرَّحْمٰنِ، الرَّح۪يمِ dört kelimedir. Hakikaten ve hükmen ise yedi kelimedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the basmala’s special orthography the alif of ism is omitted and the opening bāʾ is lengthened; frequent use explains this abbreviation, while the writing also hints at the force of connection.
rows.anchor: besmeleye mahsus olarak hemze hazf olunup söylendiği gibi yazılır ve ‘ivaz olarak ب’nin başı uzatılır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Certain hadith allusions read the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as signs of God’s splendor, radiance, and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: بَاء بَهَاءُ اللّٰهِّٰ، سِين سَنَاءُ اللّٰهِّٰ، مِيم مَمْلَكَةُ اللّٰهِّٰ gibi telmihler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾānic wisdom concerns the relation of God to the world, especially people and their acts; the basmala’s bāʾ expresses this relation of divinity and servitude.
rows.anchor: alâkasında hulâsa olunan ve evvelen Fâtiha’da, sâniyen bütün Kur’ân’da ‘ale’t-tedrîc tafsil edilen bu nisbet tamamen besmeledeki

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basic meaning of bāʾ is attachment, with senses such as accompaniment, assistance, connection, and oath; commentators read it here as accompaniment or assistance, with an omitted verb meaning begin, read, or the like.
rows.anchor: besmelede müfessirîn yalnız musâhabet veya isti‘âne mânalarından birini gösterirler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ism is originally a sign that brings something to mind and conventionally is a word denoting a meaning understood on its own; the denoted meaning or its instance is the musammā.
rows.anchor: bir mânaya delâlet eden kelime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred derivation traces ism to the root سمو, though derivation from وسم is also possible; its plurals asmāʾ and asāmī are ordinary Arabic loanwords in Turkish.
rows.anchor: Mezheb-i muhtâra göre aslı سمو maddesidir, وسم’den olması da mümkindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names include both proper and common nouns and names of entities and attributes; the distinctions matter when discussing God’s beautiful names.
rows.anchor: ism-i hâs veya ‘alem, ism-i cins veya âm diye taksim olunduğu gibi ism-i zât veya ism-i sıfat diye de tefrik olunur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turkish isim, ad, and nâm overlap but are not interchangeable in every idiom: one may say doing something in someone’s name, while some contexts favor isim for a person.
rows.anchor: lisânımızda biz bunları ince farklarla kullanırız

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is the proper personal name of the true object of worship; through this name and the divine attributes the Qurʾān introduces God and our relation to Him.
rows.anchor: Ma‘bûd-ı Hakk’ın ism-i hâssıdır. Daha doğrusu ism-i zâttır ve ism-i ‘alemdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine name is the highest organizing principle: without unity in existence, truth, and causality, the sciences remain fragmented and cannot establish even a partial truth.
rows.anchor: Vücûd, hak, nisbet-i illiyet, bütün fenlere hâkim olan mebâdî-i tasavvuriye ve tasdîkiyedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The necessary existent is the first origin and ultimate cause of both knowledge and existence; nothing that acts upon or subdues a person can be conceived without God behind it.
rows.anchor: ki onun arkasında Allah bulunmasın

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every person has an innate, simple, unbounded inner assent to God that is more truthful and powerful than finite senses, consciousness, reason, and thought because it encompasses them.
rows.anchor: bütün ilimlerimizin kökü olan bu hiss-i bâtın, mütenâhî hislerimizin, şuurlarımızın, akıllarımızın, fikirlerimizin hepsinden daha hak, hepsinden daha kuvvetlidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People’s forgetfulness of this primordial awareness is a source of error; the universe is full of divine signs and the Qurʾān recalls them with miraculous eloquence, hence its name al-Dhikr.
rows.anchor: bize bu âyâtı bir belâgat-i i‘câz ile ihtar ve tezkir ettiği için

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trying to make the encompassing divine reality into a finite object of vision is impossible: imposing a bounded endpoint on it would cut off consciousness and existence rather than yield clear vision.
rows.anchor: muhîti muhâta kalb etmeye çalışmak gibi bir nokta-i imtinâ‘vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who cannot humble their pride before God’s infinite manifestation and say they searched for God but did not find Him proclaim failure in the name of science and philosophy.
rows.anchor: fen ve felsefe nâmına hüsranlarını ilân etmiş olurlar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sensing God requires the heart to discern Him and apprehend the realized relation between them.
rows.anchor: Allah’ı sezmek için kalb ile aynı temyîz ve aralarındaki nisbet-i tahakkuku idrak edebilmelidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah denotes the divine essence as a special name or proper name: it can signify a mental concept that points to God or name the uniquely specified reality itself.
rows.anchor: Hak teâlâ’nın zâtına delâlet eden bir ism-i hâs veya bir ism-i ‘alemîdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a name is established before proving its referent, it is a proper name rather than a direct proper designation; once established after proof, it directly names the reality, illustrated by the name Ülker for blind and sighted people.
rows.anchor: ism-i hâssı olursa da ism-i ‘alemi olmaz. Fakat isbattan sonra vaz‘edilmiş ise bizzat ism-i ‘alem olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of whether God’s essence-name can be a proper designation distinguishes manifestations of essence, attributes, and effects; divine names are restricted to revelation, and direct self-manifestation is possible at least to God Himself.
rows.anchor: İsm-i zât, tecellî-i zâtı ifade eden bir isim olmak lâzım gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans cannot assign a direct proper name before experiencing a manifestation of the essence; the Qurʾān first introduces God through name-manifestations, and Rahmān and Rahīm initially unfold the name Allah.
rows.anchor: Kur’an dahi bize Allah teâlâ’yı evvelâ tecelliyât-ı ismiyesiyle anlatıyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spiritual progression passes from divine names to effects, from effects to attributes, and toward direct vision of the essence, culminating in longing for the divine encounter.
rows.anchor: Tecellî-i esmâdan tecellî-i âsâra geçeceğiz, kâinatı dolaşacağız. Tecellî-i âsârdan tecellî-i sıfâta ereceğiz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links this hoped-for encounter to the call for the tranquil soul to return to its Lord and to faces looking toward their Lord on Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: يَٰٓأَيَّتُهَا ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ ٱرْجِعِىٓ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةًۭ مَّرْضِيَّةًۭ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A concise conceptual definition of Allah is the necessary existent comprising all attributes of perfection; saying only necessary existent is sufficient because that phrase implies the perfection-attributes.
rows.anchor: O Zât-ı vâcibu’l-vücûd ki bütün sıfât-ı kemâliyeyi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah may be glossed as the true object of worship or creator of all, yet the unified meaning people hear in Allah is clearer and more complete than those definitions, making the proper-name analysis compelling.
rows.anchor: ma‘nâ-yı vahîd, bu mefhumların hepsinden daha vâzıh ve daha ekmeldir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No other object of worship is called Allah, and the name has no dual or plural; many divine names are allowed, and a proper divine name in another language is possible, though familiar Turkish names are not equivalent.
rows.anchor: Allah’tan mâ‘adâ hiçbir mâbud yâd olunmamıştır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanrı, hudā, ilāh, rabb, and maʿbūd are common nouns that can refer to false or multiple gods, so these terms cannot translate the unique proper name Allah.
rows.anchor: demek olsa yine ism-i hâs değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pluralizing Allah is false and irreverent; unlike common names for gods or revered human names, the name signifies divine unity.
rows.anchor: ism-i celâlinde böyle bir tâbir bilakis maksad-ı ta‘zîme münâfî olduğundan hem hilâf-ı hak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: French dieu is a generic, pluralizable noun; translating the declaration of faith with it yields an apparent tautology or contradiction and fails to distinguish Allah from a god, despite capitalization or Christian usage.
rows.anchor: Allah ile ilâhı temyiz edememişlerdir. Ve ikisini de ism-i hâs gibi yazmalarına rağmen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linguistic and religious historians ask whether Allah is Arabic, borrowed, derived, or primordial; the author turns to those questions while acknowledging their limits.
rows.anchor: Bu kelime esasen Arabî mi değil mi? Menkul mü mürtecel mi, müştak mı, gayr-i müştak mı?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human knowledge cannot encompass God’s essence or proper name, and Arabic has no comparable word from which its origin can be securely identified.
rows.anchor: ilmimiz Ma‘bûd-ı hakk’ın zâtını muhît olmadığı gibi ism-i hâssına karşı da öylece kāsırdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān shows that Arabs knew the name Allah and answered that Allah created the heavens and earth; its use dates at least to Ishmael, while the author finds no evidence it was borrowed from Hebrew.
rows.anchor: وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the name’s presence before Abraham may invite a Hebrew or Syriac borrowing theory, its circulation among ancient Arab peoples and earlier prophets supports an old Arabic history, with no proof of foreign borrowing.
rows.anchor: çıkan bir tarihi bulunduğu zâhirdir

rows.speaker: Basriyyûn
rows.claim: An important Basran group derives Allah from laah, a noun associated with hiding or elevation and used for divinity; the author cites Arabic poetic usage as evidence.
rows.anchor: Basriyyûn’un bir kısm-ı mühimmi bundan nakle kāil olmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinctive Arabic use of the name Allah supports its status as a unique proper name, though whether the initial alif-lām is an inseparable article and how its hamza behaves remain debated.
rows.anchor: ism-i şerîfinin lisân-ı Arab’daki hususiyeti ve binâen‘aleyh bir ism-i ‘alem olduğu anlaşılıyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib invoked God at the Kaaba during the Elephant event with laahumma, illustrating pre-Islamic use of the name; the author points readers to Sūrat al-Fīl.
rows.anchor: Abdulmuttalib hazretleri Vak‘a-i Fîl’de Kâbe kapısının halkasına yapışarak

rows.speaker: Ebû Yezîd-i Belhî
rows.claim: Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī regards laah as foreign because Jews and Christians say laha, and some relate it to Hebrew Elohim; the author says chronology cannot establish borrowing and cognate forms may share an older source.
rows.anchor: Yehûd ve Nasârâ لاها derler

rows.speaker: Kûfiyyûn
rows.claim: The Kufans derive Allah from al-ilāh, with the article becoming integral and its hamza compensating for the elided hamza of ilāh; ilāh is linked to worship, awe, tranquility, or release from fear.
rows.anchor: Kûfiyyûn bunun لاه’dan değil الاه ism-i cinsinin mürâdifi olan الاله’dan menkul olduğuna kāil olmuşlardır

rows.speaker: Zemahşerî, Kādî Beyzâvî
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, and other investigators accept the al-ilāh analysis; its meanings are gathered in the true object of worship, and the plural pattern āliha supports the proposed root.
rows.anchor: Zemahşerî, Kādî Beyzâvî gibi bir hayli muhakkikīn bu tedkīki kabul etmişlerdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two derivational analyses both preserve an original Arabic meaning in the name, though some posit a foreign origin followed by complete Arabization.
rows.anchor: bu iki tedkīke göre ismullah iştikāk-ı kebîr ile müştak olan bir ism-i Arabî’den menkuldür

rows.speaker: Ebû Hayyân-ı Endelüsî
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the majority consider Allah an un-derived, primordial proper name for the true God.
rows.anchor: ilk vaz‘ile Ma‘bûd-ı Hakk’a ism-i ‘alemdir

rows.speaker: İmam Fahreddin Râzî
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s preferred position is that Allah is God’s proper name and not originally derived; al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, many legal theorists, and jurists agree.
rows.anchor: ism-i ‘alemidir ve aslen müştak değildir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that Allah is neither derived nor transferred but was assigned primordially as a proper name; God precedes all names and attributes, and His worship-worthiness derives from Himself rather than from being worshipped.
rows.anchor: gayr-i müştak ve gayr-i menkul olup bi’l-irticâl vaz‘-ı evvelde bir ism-i ‘alemdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike idols, fire, the sun, rulers, or other things made into gods by worshippers, God remains intrinsically worthy of worship whether people recognize Him or not; even deniers are compelled to serve Him unknowingly.
rows.anchor: Allah mâbud olduğu için Allah değil, Allah olduğu için mâbuddur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By inductive reasoning proper names precede common nouns, which later arise from shared traits; therefore the claim that Allah’s name was transferred from a common noun or attribute is untenable.
rows.anchor: ism-i ‘alemler velev kısmen olsun ism-i cinslerden evvel vaz‘olunur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed compound of Hebrew El and Syriac or Arabic laah fails linguistic tests: a foreign or compound word should be indeclinable, and the proposed hamza and vowel do not match Allah’s form.
rows.anchor: kelimenin ‘ucme ve ‘alemiyetten veya terkib ve ‘alemiyetten dolayı gayr-i munsarif

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Borrowing or derivation of Allah from another language cannot be determined; like its referent, the name remains veiled in eternity, and the most basic response to it is awe and greatness.
rows.anchor: bu ism-i celâl, lisan nokta-i nazarından da müsemmâsı gibi bir ezeliyet nikābı içindedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahmān is an exclusive divine name and a dominant adjective of essence rather than action; it can occur with or without its described noun, but does not take a preposition as a verb would.
rows.anchor: Bu da Allah teâlâ’ya has bir isimdir. Bunun bir mefhûm-ı mahsûsu vardır. Fakat ism-i zât değil, ism-i sıfattır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Derived from raḥm and raḥma, Rahmān is an intensive adjective meaning possessing very abundant and enduring mercy; although analogically applicable to anyone, actual use is reserved for God.
rows.anchor: devam ve mübalağa ifade eden bir sıfat-ı müşebbehe sîgasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A flattering poet once called Musaylima rahmāna without the article, but the author says this was wrong even linguistically and all the more so religiously.
rows.anchor: Müseylimetü’l-Kezzâb’a bir kere müfrit ve müdâhin bir şâir lâmsız olarak لاَ زِلْتَ رَحْمٰنَا tâbirini kullanmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahmān can be explained as very merciful but cannot be translated as a proper divine name; esirgeyici wrongly suggests withholding or jealousy, while acıyıcı lacks the positive sense of mercy.
rows.anchor: Bu ismi belleriz ve tercemesiyle değil tefsîriyle rahmet mefhûmundan anlamaya çalışırız

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Older Turkish speakers used yarlığayıcı for mercy’s gracious result, but this remains an adjective; divine mercy itself is not an emotional inclination but the will of good or unlimited bestowal.
rows.anchor: yarlığayıcı da isim değil, sıfattır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahmān also cannot be translated as bağışlayıcı, since that confuses it with names such as Vehhāb or ʿAfūvv, which are not exclusive to God.
rows.anchor: hâs değildir. Binâen‘aleyh Rahmân, Vehhâb veya Afüvv mânalarını ifade eden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahīm is a second divine attribute, best understood here as an intensive active participle meaning very merciful or much showing mercy.
rows.anchor: iki sıfatın farkı daha bâriz olmak için burada ikincisi daha muvâfıktır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike Rahmān, Rahīm is a pure adjective, requires a described noun, can be used of others, functions verbally, and has a definite article of reference.
rows.anchor: Bu dahi Cenâb-ı Allah’ın sıfatlarından biridir. Fakat sıfat-ı mahzadır, mevsufsuz kullanılmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase moves from the pure name Allah to the name-and-attribute Rahmān and then the pure attribute Rahīm, gradually unfolding God’s name in the heart as the first manifestation of divine beauty.
rows.anchor: evvelâ bir ism-i mahz, sâniyen hem isim hem sıfat, sâlisen mahz-ı sıfat olan üç kelimeden müteşekkil olarak husustan umuma doğru inbisat etmiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators distinguish Rahmān as looking to pre-eternity and Rahīm to endless duration: creatures benefit from the former through an initial relation and from the latter through actual action at the end.
rows.anchor: lâyezâle nâzırdır. Binâen‘aleyh mahlûkât, merhamet-i Rahmâniyeden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A transmitted explanation calls God the Rahmān of this world and Rahīm of the afterlife, or the Rahmān of believers and unbelievers but Rahīm only of believers; the author clarifies that God is both names in both realms.
rows.anchor: Cenâb-ı Allah dünyanın da, âhiretin de hem rahmânı hem rahîmidir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Rahmān is God’s exclusive name, its kind of mercy and beneficence cannot issue from creatures; Rahīm is not exclusive and can describe mercy and generosity from creatures.
rows.anchor: rahmet-i Rahmân bir şart ile meşrut değil iken rahmet-i Rahîm bir şart ile meşruttur
